title: ZOMBIE Act
official_title: To reform the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 to ensure executive agencies focus on fraud prevention, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Palmer (R-AL) with no cosponsors; passed the House. Payment-integrity and fraud-prevention reforms are often bipartisan, but the lack of cosponsors and the need for 60 votes leave its Senate path uncertain.
summary: Refocuses federal improper-payment law on payments that actually cause financial loss to the government — rather than all paperwork errors — and adds fraud-risk management requirements for agencies.
brief: Reforms the Payment Integrity Information Act to focus agencies on improper payments that cause real financial loss and on fraud prevention.

top_lines.headline: Focus on Financial Loss
subs: Targets improper payments that cause actual financial loss
Excludes payments that were correct but missed paperwork steps

top_lines.headline: Fraud Risk Management
subs: Agencies adopt the GAO fraud-risk framework
Shifts some reviews from annual to every 3 years

items.main: Names the Act the “Zeroing Out Monetary Benefits Improperly Expended Act” (the “ZOMBIE Act”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Reforms to Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019

items.main: Refocuses federal improper-payment requirements on payments that result in financial loss to the government and strengthens fraud-risk management.
items.detail: Amends the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (31 U.S.C. 3351-3352). It adds a definition of 'financial loss to the Government' — payments above the legally correct amount that cause a loss, excluding correct-amount payments that missed certain administrative procedures — and reorients agency estimates, reports, and reduction plans around such payments. It requires the Treasury to develop risk-assessment guidance within one year; agencies to run risk assessments and adopt fraud-risk-management practices (including the GAO 'Framework for Managing Fraud Risks in Federal Programs'); designates agency liaisons who meet with OMB, the Treasury, Inspectors General, and the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee; requires the OMB Director and the Treasury Secretary to convene State officials responsible for program and payment integrity at least once each fiscal year to review fraud-prevention performance and share best practices; and changes several reviews and reports from annual to at least once every three years. It also amends section 3352(i)(2) to change two numeric thresholds — striking '25' and inserting '10' in subparagraph (C), and striking '25' and inserting '75' in subparagraph (D).

sections.label: Section 3 — Reforms to Annual Compliance Report by Inspectors General of Executive Agencies

items.main: Revises the Inspector General annual compliance report requirements to center on improper payments that result in financial loss to the government.
items.detail: Amends 31 U.S.C. 3353(a)(3) (OMB guidance) and 3353(a)(4) (CIGIE guidance) so that both revise their existing guidance issued under that section — rather than develop and promulgate new guidance — keyed to enactment of the ZOMBIE Act, and inserts 'that result in financial loss to the Government' throughout the related Inspectors General improper-payment provisions.

gaps: The bill narrows the focus to payments causing financial loss but does not change the penalties for improper payments.
It shifts several reviews from annual to once every three years, which could reduce how often improper payments are reassessed.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Palmer
featured_quotes.text: every year, hardworking Americans dutifully pay their taxes to support Federal public programs and other priorities. Unfortunately, the Federal Government has too often squandered their money through mismanagement. For example, just last year, the Federal Government lost an estimated $186 billion in improper payments. Six years ago, the COVID-19 pandemic produced what is now often referred to as the greatest theft of taxpayer dollars in history. This is not new.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Gill
featured_quotes.text: I encourage my colleagues to support H.R. 8467, the Zeroing Out Monetary Benefits Improperly Expended Act, which reforms the Payment Integrity Information Act to refocus Federal agencies on proactively identifying and preventing improper payments before they happen, rather than wasting resources on backward-looking compliance activities. Mr. Speaker, we need reforms like this bill that force agencies to focus on preventing improper payments in the first place, and this smart legislation does just that.

added: Definition of 'financial loss to the Government' and a Treasury risk-assessment guidance requirement within one year
modified: Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (31 U.S.C. 3351-3353) refocused on improper payments that cause financial loss, with added fraud-risk-management requirements, reforms to the Inspectors General annual compliance report, and some reviews shifted from annual to triennial

added: New Section 3 added: reforms to the annual Inspector General compliance report (section 3353) — OMB and CIGIE must revise existing guidance rather than develop new guidance, keyed to ZOMBIE Act enactment, with "financial loss to the Government" inserted throughout

New Federal-State coordination meeting: OMB Director and Treasury Secretary must convene State program- and payment-integrity officials at least once each fiscal year to review fraud-prevention performance and share best practices

Rewrites section 3352(d)(6) to require a description of how planned or completed agency actions matched the level of improper payments resulting in financial loss, with a category breakdown and specific completion timelines
modified: Section 3352(g)(2)(B) prepayment terminology now becomes "pre-award, pre-payment, and post-payment" (the introduced version had only "pre-award and pre-payment," dropping post-payment)
The statistically-valid-estimate review recommendation relocated into the high-priority report clause (subsection (b)(2)(E)(i)) instead of being added as a new subsection (b)(1)(A)
Table-of-sections conforming amendments added for the section 3352 heading changes
